> The most sensible of them said, “Did I not urge you to say, ‘Allah willing.’?”

**What "Most Sensible" Means Here**

The Arabic term rendered *most sensible* can also be read as the most balanced, the most equitable, or the most just among them, and the commentators leaned on both senses. The word describes a person who occupies the middle of a matter instead of an extreme, and the sūrah applies it to the man whose counsel earlier would have prevented the disaster. A group in crisis contains people of different quality, and the Book is precise about which kind speaks. What he says is not an accusation about the harvest; it is an appeal to something he had offered before there was any reason to remember it.

The quality the verse praises has a public use in the Book. The community is told that it has been made an upright one so that it may stand as a witness over humanity: *“And so We have made you ˹believers˺ an upright community so that you may be witnesses over humanity…”* (2:143). The word behind *upright* carries the same sense of the middle that the verse gives to *most sensible*. Balance in this vocabulary is not the avoidance of a position; it is the footing a person needs to say the true thing while the people around him are stumbling.

**The Advice That Had Been Dropped**

His question refers to the rule the Book lays down about statements about the future: *“And never say of anything, “I will definitely do this tomorrow,” without adding, “if Allah so wills!” But if you forget, then remember your Lord. Say, “I trust my Lord will guide me to what is more right than this.””* (18:23–24). The practice is not a formula for softening a promise. It is the acknowledgement that the person speaking is not the one who decides which morning arrives, and it belongs most naturally to a man making plans about a harvest.

**"Why Do You Not Glorify?"**

In the fuller wording of the tradition the question is asked with the verb for glorification, and the commentators understood it as an appeal to give thanks and to attribute the blessing to God rather than to the family's own effort. The Book's diagnosis of the opposite habit is stated in a passage about prosperity and scarcity: *“Now, whenever a human being is tested by their Lord through ˹His˺ generosity and blessings, they boast, “My Lord has ˹deservedly˺ honoured me!” But when He tests them by limiting their provision, they protest, “My Lord has ˹undeservedly˺ humiliated me!””* (89:15–16).

**Reminders Remembered at the Gate**

The Book reports that human beings call on God when hardship arrives and forget the appeal once it is lifted: *“Whenever someone is touched by hardship, they cry out to Us, whether lying on their side, sitting, or standing. But when We relieve their hardship, they return to their old ways as if they had never cried to Us to remove any hardship!”* (10:12).
verses.29:
> They replied, “Glory be to our Lord! We have truly been wrongdoers.”

**The First Right Sentence in the Story**

The family that whispered on the road and argued at the gate finally says something that is completely true. The words pair two movements. The first is the glorification of God, which declares Him free of any fault in what happened. The second is an admission about themselves: they were wrongdoers, and the sentence does not qualify the claim with excuses. After three verses of confusion, argument, and mutual blame, the group arrives at the vocabulary the Book has been preparing them for. The sūrah reports the sentence in the plural, so the confession is made by the whole family rather than by one of its members.

**Glorification and Confession Joined Together**

The two halves of the sentence belong to each other. Praise directed at God removes the possibility that the disaster was unjust, and the confession directed at themselves gives up the possibility that they were merely unlucky. The Book uses the combination in the mouths of nations that had already been destroyed: *“Their only cry—when overwhelmed by Our torment—was, “We have indeed been wrongdoers.””* (7:5). A similar scene appears in the sūrah of the Prophets: *“They cried, “Woe to us! We have surely been wrongdoers.” They kept repeating their cry until We mowed them down, ˹leaving them˺ lifeless.”* (21:14–15).

One further verse makes the point with an image that could have been written about the brothers: *“If they were touched by even a breath of your Lord's torment, they would certainly cry, “Woe to us! We have really been wrongdoers.””* (21:46). The confession is the human being's most natural response to being caught, and the Book records it in the same words in every century.

**The Confession in This Life and the Confession in the Fire**

The Book gives the same words to people whose situation is already decided, and it is careful about the difference. Confession in this world is the door out of a wrong; the same words spoken in the next world are simply the record being agreed to. The sūrah's brothers have lost their garden but not their lives, and the passage that follows this one contains a hope that would have no place in a scene of final judgement: they trust that their Lord will give them something better than what they had (68:32 — *“We trust our Lord will give us a better garden than this, ˹for˺ we are indeed turning to our Lord with hope.””*).
verses.30:
> Then they turned on each other, throwing blame

**Why Reproach Makes the Torment Worse**

The Book treats mutual blame as part of the punishment rather than as relief from it. Two verses make the point in the plainest terms: those who misled others will disown their followers when the torment appears and every bond between them will be cut (2:166 — *“˹Consider the Day˺ when those who misled others will disown their followers—when they face the torment—and the bonds that united them will be cut off”*). The followers will wish for a second chance so that they could disown their leaders as they were disowned, and God will make them remorseful of their deeds without letting them leave (2:167 — *“The ˹misled˺ followers will cry, “If only we could have a second chance, we would disown them as they disowned us.””*). Nothing in the exchange changes the situation of either party, and nothing in it consoles anyone.

**Blame as the Book's Signature of the Exposed**

The Qur'an repeatedly describes people under judgement as occupied with each other's faults. The followers in the Fire appeal to the leaders who had misled them: *“We were your ˹dedicated˺ followers, will you then shield us from a portion of the Fire?”*, and the answer they receive is a refusal: *“We are all in it! ˹For˺ Allah has already passed judgment over ˹His˺ servants.”* (40:47–48). In another passage the lowly and the arrogant are set against each other in the same way: the followers say that without their leaders they would have believed, and the leaders reply that they had not hindered anyone from guidance (34:31–32 — *“The lowly ˹followers˺ will say to the arrogant ˹leaders˺, “Had it not been for you, we would certainly have been believers.””*). The exchange continues until the followers accuse the leaders of plotting by day and night, and the verse ends by noting that all of them conceal their remorse when they see the punishment (34:33 — *“The lowly will say to the arrogant, “No!”*).

The Book records a version of the same scene between relatives: friends who were partners in wrongdoing become each other's accusers, and the exception is the righteous (43:67 — *“Close friends will be enemies to one another on that Day, except the righteous”*).

There is also a social cost that the passage leaves for the reader to calculate. Every hour spent in reproach was a hour in which the household's actual situation went unaddressed: what remained of the estate, what the families would eat, whether any part of the ground could be replanted. The Book's descriptions of the Hereafter use the same material for a different reason, showing that blame in the presence of a settled verdict is not only unhelpful but a continuation of the offence that produced the verdict.

**The Dispute That Has Already Been Answered**

Another passage shows what such arguments sound like when the record is produced: *“Allah will respond, “Do not dispute in My presence, since I had already given you a warning.””* (50:28). The subject of the argument is closed before anyone speaks, and the parties are left in the position of men continuing a case whose verdict they are holding in their hands.

**What Households Argue About After a Disaster**

There is a recognisable human anatomy to what the passage describes. A family facing a serious loss rarely argues about the original decision; it argues about who first suggested it, who failed to object, and who should have known better. The man who gave good advice (68:28 — *“The most sensible of them said, “Did I not urge you to say, ‘Allah willing.’?””*) has already reminded the group of what he had said, and the argument that follows his reminder is a try to respond to that reminder without accepting it.

The dispute about blame is being conducted on ground that was completely their own creation, and the accusation they trade — that someone failed to help the poor — is the one criticism of which every member of the group is guilty.

> They said, “Woe to us! We have certainly been transgressors

**"Woe to Us": the Cry of a Recognised Verdict**

The word rendered *woe* is the Book's own exclamation of regret, and it appears wherever people discover that a matter has been settled against them. When the record of deeds is laid open, the wicked cry out in the same terms and ask what kind of book leaves nothing out: *“They will cry, “Woe to us! What kind of record is this that does not leave any sin, small or large, unlisted?” They will find whatever they did present ˹before them˺. And your Lord will never wrong anyone.”* (18:49). At the resurrection the same cry goes up as people are raised from their resting places (36:52 — *“They will cry, “Woe to us! Who has raised us up from our place of rest? This must be what the Most Compassionate warned us of; the messengers told the truth!””*), and at the arrival of the Day of Judgement it is the first thing the disbelievers say (37:20 — *“They will cry, “Oh, woe to us! This is the Day of Judgment!””*).

**A Confession With No Request Attached**

Nothing follows the admission. There is no plea for the garden, no offer to compensate anyone, and no try to bargain over the outcome. The Book contains confessions of that other kind, including the one that is expressly excluded from acceptance: the repentance of a person who continues in his conduct until death arrives and then says that he repents (4:18 — *“However, repentance is not accepted from those who knowingly persist in sin until they start dying, and then cry, “Now I repent!” nor those who die as disbelievers.”*). The brothers' sentence belongs to the same family of statements, with one important difference — the men are still alive, and the verses that follow show what the Book does with a confession made in time.

The narrative gives the family several tries at understanding what happened: they thought they had taken the wrong road (v26), then named their deprivation (v27), then called themselves wrongdoers (v29), and now transgressors.

**Regret That Arrives in Time**

The Book distinguishes sharply between regret that can be acted on and regret that cannot. A verse states the door plainly: *“Whoever commits evil or wrongs themselves then seeks Allah's forgiveness will certainly find Allah All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”* (4:110). Another describes the repentance that is accepted as the repentance of those who err and then turn soon afterwards (4:17 — *“Allah only accepts the repentance of those who commit evil ignorantly ˹or recklessly˺ then repent soon after—Allah will pardon them. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise”*). The brothers at the gate have lost their harvest and have not lost their lives, and the sūrah places their cry on the right side of that line without making a speech about it.

Regret in the Book is therefore measured by what it produces rather than by how strongly it is felt. The cry of *woe* can belong to a person who never repents at all — it is the sound the wicked make when the record is opened — or it can be the first sentence of a life that changes direction. What decides the case is whether anything follows the sentence, and in this story something does.

**What the Reader Is Meant to Do With the Cry**

A reader who has followed the passage from the oath to the gate has heard the family say everything that a person says when it is too late to change the outcome. The Book's purpose in reporting those sentences is not to make the reader feel the men's regret; it is to put the same words in front of him while he still has options. The revelation asks for the turn that the brothers have just made, and it asks for it earlier: *“O believers! Turn to Allah in sincere repentance, so your Lord may absolve you of your sins and admit you into Gardens, under which rivers flow.”* (66:8).

> We trust our Lord will give us a better garden than this, ˹for˺ we are indeed turning to our Lord with hope.”

**Hope Arrives With the Confession**

The family's turn produces a sentence about the future. Having admitted what they were, they state their expectation of their Lord, and the verse puts the two movements in a single line so that neither stands alone. The Book consistently joins the confession of a wrong with an opening rather than a verdict, even where the consequences of the wrong remain in place. A ruined garden is not undone by repentance; a relationship is restored by it, and the verse treats the second restoration as the one that matters at the gate.

**"Better Than This" and the Book's Arithmetic of Loss**

The claim is bold in its setting. What the brothers lost was a productive estate, and they say in the middle of the wreckage that they expect their Lord to give them something better. The Book makes the same offer repeatedly, and it does so with the contrast between what passes and what remains: *“Whatever you have will end, but whatever Allah has is everlasting. And We will certainly reward the steadfast according to the best of their deeds.”* (16:96). The next verse of that sūrah widens the promise to cover the conditions of living: *“Whoever does good, whether male or female, and is a believer, We will surely bless them with a good life, and We will certainly reward them according to the best of their deeds.”* (16:97).

Other passages state the same principle for people recovering from serious failure: those who believe and do good will have their misdeeds replaced by something better (29:7 — *“As for those who believe and do good, We will certainly absolve them of their sins, and reward them according to the best of what they used to do”*), and forgiveness is followed by a reward measured by the best of what a person has done (39:35 — *“As such, Allah will absolve them of ˹even˺ the worst of what they did and reward them according to the best of what they used to do”*). The brothers' hope is not optimism about weather or land; it is confidence in the character of the one they are addressing.

**"Turning to Our Lord" and the Practice Behind the Word**

The Arabic term rendered *turning* describes a movement of return that is expected to repeat rather than to occur once. The same description is given to Abraham in the Qur'an, who is called ever turning to his Lord (11:75 — *“Truly, Abraham was forbearing, tender-hearted, and ever turning ˹to his Lord˺”*), and it recurs in the Book as a title for people whose direction of travel has been corrected. The brothers describe themselves with that word rather than with the vocabulary of a completed transaction. What they are announcing at the gate is a change of orientation — away from the estate and the plan and toward the one who owns both.
