> That is the ˹way of Our˺ punishment ˹in this world˺. But the punishment of the Hereafter is certainly far worse, if only they knew

**Punishment in This World as a Warning**

The Book treats loss and hardship in this life as instruments that are meant to bring people back rather than to finish them. One verse states the intention explicitly: *“We will certainly make them taste some of the minor torment ˹in this life˺ before the major torment ˹of the Hereafter˺, so perhaps they will return ˹to the Right Path˺.”* (32:21). Another verse assigns the cause of affliction to human conduct while noting how much is forgiven: *“Whatever affliction befalls you is because of what your own hands have committed. And He pardons much.”* (42:30).

**Miserliness as the Charge Against the Deniers**

The commentators connect the parable's crime to the fate described in this verse and explain that the disbelievers are being warned about their own hoarding. The Book's portrait of the miser is one of its sharpest: *“Woe to every backbiter, slanderer, who amasses wealth ˹greedily˺ and counts it ˹repeatedly˺, thinking that their wealth will make them immortal!”* (104:1–3). The final clause identifies the underlying belief. A person who hoards is not simply failing to share; he is treating his store as a guarantee against the mortality he cannot escape.

The warning to the same behaviour appears in the sūrah of Repentance with an image that matches the brothers' situation: those who hoard gold and silver without spending it in God's cause are told that their treasure will be heated in the fire and used to brand their foreheads, sides. Backs, with the words *“This is the treasure you hoarded for yourselves. Now taste what you hoarded!”* (9:34–35). What a person refuses to release is returned to him as an instrument of his own punishment.

**Why the Hereafter's Punishment Is Called Greater**

The comparison in this verse is not between two penalties of similar kind but between two orders of magnitude. A farmer who loses a crop loses a season; the accounting that follows this life concerns the whole of what a person was. The Book makes the contrast in a sentence that borrows the same structure as the verse before us: *“So Allah made them taste humiliation in this worldly life, but far worse is the punishment of the Hereafter, if only they knew.”* (39:26). The humiliation mentioned there is one nation's experience of being brought down in the world, and the Book's point is that the same people face something considerably heavier.

For the sūrah's first audience, the visible scale mattered. Makkan society measured standing in camels, gardens, and alliances, and the verse insists that the accounting on the other side is not measured in those units at all.
verses.34:
> Indeed, the righteous will have the Gardens of Bliss with their Lord

**What the Word "Bliss" Names**

The gardens in this verse are gardens of *naʿīm*, and the commentators explain the term as blessing that is pure and unmixed, in contrast to the goods of this world, which arrive attached to anxieties, conditions, and the risk of loss. The Book uses the word repeatedly for the opposite of punishment: the virtuous are described as being in bliss while the wicked are in a blazing fire (82:13–14 — *“Indeed, the virtuous will be in bliss”*). The same picture is drawn in the sūrah of the Defrauders, where the virtuous are seated on couches and the glow of delight is visible on their faces (83:22–24 — *“You will recognize on their faces the glow of delight”*). In another sūrah the people of that bliss are described as fully pleased with what their striving produced, and the sūrah names their dwelling as an elevated garden (88:8–10 — *“in an elevated Garden”*).

One passage places the same word in the middle of the journey rather than at its end, promising serenity, fragrance, and a garden of bliss to the soul of the person brought near to God (56:88–89 — *“then ˹such a person will have˺ serenity, fragrance, and a Garden of Bliss”*). Bliss in the Qur'an's vocabulary is a condition, not merely a place.

**"With Their Lord": the Phrase That Fixes the Value**

The gardens are not described as a distant inheritance but as being *with* the Lord of the righteous, and the Book's descriptions of the reward return to that nearness as the highest part of it. The people of paradise are said to be at the seat of honour in the presence of the Sovereign (54:55 — *“at the Seat of Honour in the presence of the Most Powerful Sovereign”*), and other passages describe faces that are pleased because they are looking at their Lord. A reader who understands the gardens as a set of pleasures has missed the phrase in this verse, which locates the reward in a relationship before it locates it in a landscape.

That is also the answer to the sūrah's earlier story. The garden in the parable was a possession that its owners stood outside of; the gardens promised here are described in relation to their owner as much as their occupants.

**Righteousness Defined by Conduct, Not by Wealth**

The verse names the people who receive the gardens as the righteous, and the Book elsewhere explains what the term covers. A long verse sets out the definition while explicitly denying that it can be reduced to ritual direction: *“Righteousness is not in turning your faces toward the east or the west. Rather, the righteous are those who believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Books. The prophets; who give charity out of their cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, the poor, ˹needy˺ travellers, beggars, and for freeing captives; who establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and keep the pledges they make; and who are patient in times of suffering, adversity, and in ˹the heat of˺ battle.”* (2:177).

**What the Promise Meant to the First Believers**

The community hearing this sūrah held little of what Makkah counted as wealth. Its members were drawn from the poorer families of the city, from those without protection, and from a few men who had given up their standing. A promise of gardens with their Lord was an answer to their circumstances which did not involve becoming like the men who opposed them. The Book reinforces the point elsewhere by promising that God will never waste the work of anyone who migrates, is expelled, or is persecuted for His sake, and by naming the reward as gardens beneath which rivers flow (3:195 — *“Both are equal in reward. Those who migrated or were expelled from their homes, and were persecuted for My sake and fought and ˹some˺ were martyred—I will certainly forgive their sins and admit them into Gardens under which rivers flow, as a reward from Allah.”*).
verses.35:
> Should We then treat those who have submitted like the wicked

**The Same Question Elsewhere in the Book**

Other passages make the same comparison with variations in vocabulary, and the repetition shows how central the argument is. One verse asks the question in two forms at once: *“Or should We treat those who believe and do good like those who make mischief throughout the land? Or should We treat the righteous like the wicked?”* (38:28). Another states the matter as a plain fact rather than a question: *“Is the one who is a believer equal ˹before Allah˺ to the one who is rebellious? They are not equal!”* (32:18). A third keeps both pairs together: *“Those blind ˹to the truth˺ and those who can see are not equal, nor are those who believe and do good ˹equal˺ to those who do evil. Yet you are hardly mindful.”* (40:58).

The Book also extends the comparison into imagery of light and darkness, heat and shade, and life and death (35:19–22 — *“nor are the darkness and the light”*), each pair making the same claim about the difference between two conditions that look similar from outside.

One more verse places the same distinction in a command rather than a question, and it directs the audience to the standard rather than the appearance: *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Good and evil are not equal, though you may be dazzled by the abundance of evil.””* (5:100). The sūrah's question in this verse is the same question with its details removed, which is why it can be answered by anyone who has ever watched an unjust man prosper and found the sight intolerable.

**The Two Words: Submitted and Wicked**

The verse contrasts people who have *submitted* with people it calls *wicked*, and the second term is a legal and moral category rather than an insult. The commentators note that the word for the submitters here is the same word used for Muslims, and some of them observe that this may be the earliest appearance of the term in the order of revelation. The pairing is therefore exact: on one side are people who handed their affairs to God, and on the other are people whose conduct made them answerable for a crime. The verse asks whether the two are to be equivalent, and the question assumes that the audience will find the idea unacceptable.

**Justice as the Ground of the Question**

Nothing in the verse defends the distinction it draws by appealing to privilege. Its argument is the opposite: the Book treats the difference between the two groups as a requirement of justice. A judge who punished the obedient and the criminal alike would be regarded as unfair by every human standard, and the verse uses that common standard against the people who were demanding to be judged differently. The final accounting in the Book is described in the language of scales and exact weights, with the assurance that no soul will be wronged by so much as a mustard seed (21:47 — *“We will set up the scales of justice on the Day of Judgment, so no soul will be wronged in the least.”*).
verses.36:
> What is the matter with you? How do you judge

**A Rebuke in Two Questions**

The verse follows the comparison with an expression of astonishment, and it directs the astonishment at the audience rather than at the argument. The first question asks what has happened to them; the second asks about the quality of the judgment they are applying. In two short sentences the sūrah moves from the content of the claim to the condition of the people making it, which is where the Book usually locates the real problem. The audience has just been told that the righteous and the wicked are not alike, and their objection to the statement is itself being placed under examination.

Questions of this kind recur in the Qur'an whenever a group substitutes its own preferences for a standard. The Book asks what has happened to an audience's reasoning, and then asks how they have arrived at their verdict. The sūrah has already used the second question once in a related form, and it will return to the same challenge in the verses that follow, where the audience is asked whether they have a scripture, an oath, or a guarantor that supports their expectations (68:37–41 — *“Or do you have a scripture, in which you read that you will have whatever you choose Or do you have oaths binding on Us until the Day of Judgment that you will have whatever you decide Ask them ˹O Prophet˺ which of them can guarantee all that Or do they have associate-gods ˹supporting this claim˺? Then let them bring forth their associate-gods, if what they say is true”*). The series works as a courtroom sequence in which the defendants are asked to produce their documents and cannot.

**The Faculty They Were Supposed to Use**

The Book's appeal is not to blind obedience but to a capacity the audience was given and knows it has. One verse states the contrast with the same vocabulary the sūrah has used earlier: *“˹Are they better˺ or those who worship ˹their Lord˺ devoutly in the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of their Lord? Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Are those who know equal to those who do not know?” None will be mindful ˹of this˺ except people of reason.”* (39:9). The Book elsewhere describes wisdom itself as a gift from God and adds that only people of understanding take the reminder (2:269 — *“But none will be mindful ˹of this˺ except people of reason”*).

An earlier verse of the Book describes the danger of judging by what is plentiful rather than by what is true: *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Good and evil are not equal, though you may be dazzled by the abundance of evil. So be mindful of Allah, O people of reason, so you may be successful.””* (5:100). The Makkan elite were dazzled by abundance in the most literal sense. They had the numbers, the income, and the alliances, and they concluded from the size of their position that the position was correct.
verses.37:
> Or do you have a scripture, in which you read

**The Book They Were Ignoring**

The sūrah's question lands differently when read beside the verses that describe what a scripture demands. One passage defines the people who actually have revelation as those who follow it as it should be followed (2:121 — *“Those We have given the Book follow it as it should be followed. It is they who ˹truly˺ believe in it. As for those who reject it, it is they who are the losers”*), and another asks what message an audience will believe in after denying God and His revelations (45:6 — *“These are Allah’s revelations which We recite to you ˹O Prophet˺ in truth. So what message will they believe in after ˹denying˺ Allah and His revelations”*). The Makkans had no book of their own to consult about the next world, and they had access to the one that had been recited in their streets for years. The question in this verse simply makes that arrangement explicit.

The sūrah moves from asking how the deniers judge to asking what they are reading. The question is whether they have a revealed book that supports their expectation of being treated differently from the righteous, and it is put in the form of a challenge rather than a proposition.

**The Book's Habit of Asking for Proof**

This kind of challenge recurs throughout the Qur'an whenever a group claims a position that the revelation does not grant it. One verse demands the evidence directly: *“Bring me a scripture ˹revealed˺ before this ˹Quran˺ or a shred of knowledge, if what you say is true.”* (46:4). Another turns the claim back on the claimants with the same instrument: *“Then bring ˹us˺ your scripture, if what you say is true!”* (37:157). A third asks whether such a book exists at all and whether its owners are holding to it: *“Or have We given them a Book ˹for proof˺, before this ˹Quran˺, to which they are holding firm?”* (43:21).

Two further passages supply the context of the Makkan claim. The Book notes that no scripture had been sent to these people to study and no warner had come to them before (34:44 — *“˹They say so even though˺ We had never given them any scriptures to study, nor did We ever send them a warner before you ˹O Prophet˺”*), and it asks their associate-gods to show what they have created, ending with the observation that the wrongdoers promise each other nothing but delusion (35:40 — *“In fact, the wrongdoers promise each other nothing but delusion.””*).

**A Community Without a Book of Its Own**

The Book states its own status in the same connection: it was revealed as an authority in Arabic, and following the desires of a community after knowledge has arrived leaves a person without a protector (13:37 — *“And so We have revealed it as an authority in Arabic.”*).

**Reading Selectively From a Book**

The idea of a scripture that grants a reader his choice appears elsewhere in the Book as a description of how some communities handled their revelations. One verse describes people who know nothing of the Book except what they wish to be true, and who deal only in conjecture (2:78 — *“And among them are the illiterate who know nothing about the Scripture except lies, and ˹so˺ they ˹wishfully˺ speculate”*). Another addresses a group that believed part of the scripture and rejected the rest, asking what reward such conduct deserves beyond disgrace in this world and the harshest punishment on the Day of Judgment (2:85 — *“Do you believe in some of the Scripture and reject the rest?”*). A third reports those who distorted the words of the Book with their tongues and attributed the result to God (3:78 — *“There are some among them who distort the Book with their tongues to make you think this ˹distortion˺ is from the Book—but it is not what the Book says.”*).

The question in this sūrah belongs to that family of criticisms. It asks whether the audience's expectation of exemption came from a text they had received or from a preference they had brought with them.
verses.38:
> that you will have whatever you choose

**The Method of Taking a Claim to its Conclusion**

The Book's treatment of the deniers is often conducted by following their assumptions to a destination they would not have chosen. The sūrah has already asked whether the righteous and the wicked are to be treated alike; here it asks whether the audience's position rests on a document granting them whatever they want. Neither question invents a claim. Each one states the logical outcome of what the audience already believed, and the sūrah lets the absurdity of the outcome speak for itself.

The audience's real position is one the Book names in another sūrah: those who follow nothing but assumptions and do nothing but lie (6:116 — *“˹O Prophet!˺ If you were to obey most of those on earth, they would lead you away from Allah’s Way. They follow nothing but assumptions and do nothing but lie”*).

The verse raises a question that runs through the whole revelation about the source of a person's judgments. A verse warns against declaring things lawful and unlawful with the tongue to fabricate claims about God (16:116 — *“Do not falsely declare with your tongues, “This is lawful, and that is unlawful,””*), and another asks whether the audience is seeking the judgment of pre-Islamic ignorance when a better judge exists for people of sure faith (5:50 — *“Is it the judgment of ˹pre-Islamic˺ ignorance they seek? Who could be a better judge than Allah for people of sure faith”*). The Book's objection in both places is the same as the objection here. A standard that changes with a person's wishes is not a standard; it is a preference wearing the clothes of a rule.

The Makkan audience would have recognised the argument, because their own commercial law depended on standards that did not bend according to the parties involved.

**The Hereafter Is Not Open to Negotiation**

Several verses in the Qur'an place the final judgment beyond the reach of human preference. One asks whether the audience seeks a judge other than the One who revealed the Book explained completely, while those who received earlier scriptures know the revelation to be true (6:114 — *“˹Say, O Prophet,˺ “Should I seek a judge other than Allah while He is the One Who has revealed for you the Book ˹with the truth˺ perfectly explained?””*). Another states that following the desires of others after knowledge has arrived leaves a person with no protector and no shield (13:37 — *“And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge that has come to you, there would be none to protect or shield you from Allah”*). A third compares the two parties in the clearest possible terms: *“Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Can any of your associate-gods guide to the truth?” Say, “˹Only˺ Allah guides to the truth.” Who then is more worthy to be followed: the One Who guides to the truth or those who cannot find the way unless guided? What is the matter with you? How do you judge?””* (10:35).

That verse ends with the same rebuke the sūrah under discussion has just used, which shows how closely the two passages are related in method and in subject.

**What the Followers of Revelation Receive Instead**

The alternative to choosing is described in the Book as submission, and the term is not a surrender of dignity. The people who are given the Book and follow it properly are described as the ones who truly believe it (2:121 — *“Those We have given the Book follow it as it should be followed. It is they who ˹truly˺ believe in it. As for those who reject it, it is they who are the losers”*). A verse about the prophets explains that a man blessed with scripture would never instruct people to worship him; he would call them to be devoted to their Lord in accordance with what is read and taught (3:79 — *“Rather, he would say, “Be devoted to the worship of your Lord ˹alone˺”—in accordance with what these prophets read in the Scripture and what they taught”*). The submission the Book asks for is directed at a text and a Lord, and it leaves the person who practises it with more certainty about his future than any audience of self-made promises has ever had.
verses.39:
> Or do you have oaths binding on Us until the Day of Judgment that you will have whatever you decide

**Oaths in the Book's Portrait of Makkah**

The Book reports the oaths of this community with a consistency that amounts to a portrait. People swore their most solemn oaths that God would never raise the dead (16:38 — *“They swear by Allah their most solemn oaths that Allah will never raise the dead to life. Yes ˹He will˺! It is a true promise binding on Him, but most people do not know”*).

They swore that a warner would make them better guided than any other community, and the warning made them worse (35:42 — *“They swore by Allah their most solemn oaths that if a warner were to come to them, they would certainly be better guided than any other community.”*); they swore that a sign would make them believe (6:109 — *“What will make you ˹believers˺ realize that even if a sign were to come to them, they still would not believe”*); they swore to the believers to please them (9:62 — *“They swear by Allah to you ˹believers˺ in order to please you, while it is the pleasure of Allah and His Messenger they should seek, if they are ˹true˺ believers”*); they swore that if commanded they would march forth (24:53 — *“They swear by Allah their most solemn oaths that if you ˹O Prophet˺ were to command them, they would certainly march forth ˹in Allah’s cause˺.”*). The hypocrites of Madinah likewise used their oaths as a shield and swore to lies knowingly (58:14 — *“And they swear to lies knowingly”*, 58:16 — *“They have made their ˹false˺ oaths as a shield, hindering ˹others˺ from the cause of Allah. So they will suffer a humiliating punishment”*; 63:2 — *“They have made their ˹false˺ oaths as a shield, hindering ˹others˺ from the Way of Allah. Evil indeed is what they do”*).

**Books Read as Guarantees of Safety**

The attitude this verse attacks has a history in the Book. One passage reports a claim of limited punishment, and the answer it receives is exactly the question being asked here: *“˹Some of˺ the Jews claim, “The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Have you taken a pledge from Allah— for Allah never breaks His word—or are you ˹just˺ saying about Allah what you do not know?””* (2:80). The question distinguishes sharply between two cases. A pledge from God is unbreakable and must therefore be found somewhere in what He has revealed; a claim for which no such pledge exists is a statement about God made without knowledge.

Another passage extends the same challenge to the Makkans and their claim of superiority: *“Now, are you ˹Meccan˺ disbelievers superior to those ˹destroyed peoples˺? Or have you ˹been granted˺ immunity ˹from punishment˺ in divine Books?”* (54:43). Immunity of that kind appears nowhere in the scriptures, and the sūrah's question assumes that the audience knows it.

Against casual swearing the Book sets a severe valuation of the oath itself: whoever trades God's covenant and his oaths for a fleeting gain will have no share in the Hereafter (3:77 — *“Indeed, those who trade Allah’s covenant and their oaths for a fleeting gain will have no share in the Hereafter.”*), and deliberate oaths carry an expiation for the person who breaks them (5:89 — *“This is the penalty for breaking your oaths.”*). An oath in this society was not a figure of speech, which is why the question in this verse is so damaging.

The chapter's opening words are themselves an oath, and the direction of the two arrangements is what this verse exposes: *“Nũn. By the pen and what everyone writes!”* (68:1).

**What the Audience Is Left Holding**

The demand for evidence is one the Book makes of every community that has staked a claim on the Hereafter: *“The Jews and Christians each claim that none will enter Paradise except those of their own faith. These are their desires. Reply, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Show ˹me˺ your proof if what you say is true.””* (2:111). The claim in each case is the same in shape — a group treating its identity as a title deed — and the answer is the same request for the paperwork.

The Book's own account of authority is stated in a sentence from the sūrah of the Cattle: the punishment the mockers wished to hasten is not within any human power to deliver, and it is God alone who decides its time (6:57 — *“It is only Allah Who decides ˹its time˺.”*).
verses.40:
> Ask them ˹O Prophet˺ which of them can guarantee all that

**From Documents to Persons**

The sūrah shifts the demand from texts to people. Having asked whether the audience has a book or a pledge, the verse instructs the Prophet ﷺ to ask whether any of them will stand behind the claim, and the commentators explain the word rendered *guarantee* as a form of the verb for taking responsibility for what one has said. The three supports the audience might have cited have now been identified: a revelation, a promise from God, or a superior reward in the next life. The question asks who among them has received any of it.

**The Claim Confronted With Its Claimants**

A group's position often looks stronger than the individuals who hold it, and the sūrah separates the two. Asking which of them can vouch for the expectation reduces a communal conviction to a personal undertaking, and the Book uses this method in several places. When the Makkans were asked about the creation of the heavens and the earth, they answered that the Almighty, the All-Knowing had created them (43:9 — *“If you ask them ˹O Prophet˺ who created the heavens and the earth, they will certainly say, “The Almighty, All-Knowing did.””*); asked to whom the earth and everyone on it belonged, they answered that it was God's (23:84–85 — *“Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “To whom belong the earth and all those on it, if you ˹really˺ know?””*). Their own testimony was available to them in matters they could see, and the guarantee they were asked for in this verse concerns a matter they had no access to at all.

The audience's error was not a lack of information about God's existence; it was the assumption that their relationship with Him had been settled in their favour without terms. The Book records the Prophet's ﷺ own position on the limits of his knowledge in a verse from another sūrah: knowledge of the Hour rests with God alone, and the messenger's task is to warn (79:44–45 — *“That knowledge rests with your Lord ˹alone˺”*). A man who stated that limit about himself was in a poor position to accept a guarantee from men who claimed no limit at all.

**Guarantors Withdrawn From the Scene**

The Book's descriptions of the Last Day systematically remove the figures whom people had counted on to speak for them. Intercession is said to belong to God alone (39:44 — *“Say, “All intercession belongs to Allah ˹alone˺. To Him belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth. Then to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned.””*), and the day is described as one on which no friendship will be of use (2:254 — *“O believers! Donate from what We have provided for you before the arrival of a Day when there will be no bargaining, friendship, or intercession.”*). The sūrah's next verse continues the same process by asking the audience whether they have associate-gods and inviting them to produce them. The demand for a guarantor in this verse is therefore not a rhetorical flourish; it is the first step in a process that the sūrah completes over the following verses.

**The Promise God Did Make**

The Book does contain promises, and it states their conditions. One verse describes the consequence of trading God's covenant and oaths for a temporary advantage: no share in the Hereafter, no speech from God, no glance, no purification, and a painful punishment (3:77 — *“And they will suffer a painful punishment”*). Another states the positive form: whoever fulfils the pledge he has made to God will receive a great reward (48:10 — *“And whoever fulfils their pledge to Allah, He will grant them a great reward”*). What the sūrah's audience wanted was a guarantee without a pledge of their own, and the Book's promises run in the opposite direction.
verses.41:
> Or do they have associate-gods ˹supporting this claim˺? Then let them bring forth their associate-gods, if what they say is true

**The Day They Are Called and Do Not Answer**

In one passage the Prophet ﷺ is told to address the idolaters directly: *“Do they have feet to walk with? Or hands to hold with? Or eyes to see with? Or ears to hear with? Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Call upon your associate-gods and conspire against me without delay!””* (7:195).

**Gods That Cannot Create or Help Themselves**

The Qur'an's descriptions of the idols strip them of every capacity their worshippers assumed. One verse lists what they cannot do in a single sentence: *“Yet they have taken besides Him gods who cannot create anything but are themselves created. Nor can they protect or benefit themselves. Nor can they control life, death, or resurrection.”* (25:3). Another pairs the charge with two questions: *“Do they associate ˹with Allah˺ those ˹idols˺ which cannot create anything, but are in fact created; which cannot help them, or even help themselves?”* (7:191–192).

The sūrah of the Spider supplies the image the Book uses for the whole arrangement: those who take protectors other than God are like a spider spinning a shelter, and the flimsiest of shelters is that of a spider (29:41 — *“The parable of those who take protectors other than Allah is that of a spider spinning a shelter.”*). The picture is not of wickedness but of structural weakness, and the verse under discussion asks the audience to lean on the structure in public.

**Intercessors Who Cannot Even Testify**

The Makkan claim was not usually that the idols created or ruled; it was that they carried requests to God. The Book answers that claim in a series of verses that remove the intercessors from the picture. One verse reports the audience's own explanation of their worship and asks whether they are informing God of something He does not know (10:18 — *“Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Are you informing Allah of something He does not know in the heavens or the earth?”*). Another asks whether they have taken intercessors who have neither authority nor intelligence (39:43 — *“Or have they taken others besides Allah as intercessors? Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “˹Would they do so,˺ even though those ˹idols˺ have neither authority nor intelligence?””*). A third observes that the beings people call upon besides God cannot even respond, and are unaware that they are being called (46:5 — *“And who could be more astray than those who call upon others besides Allah—˹others˺ that cannot respond to them until the Day of Judgment, and are ˹even˺ unaware of their calls”*).

The Book describes what happens when the arrangement is finally tested. In one scene the disbelievers are told to call upon their associate-gods, they call, and no answer comes (28:64 — *“It will be said ˹to the disbelievers˺, “Call upon your associate-gods ˹for help˺.””*); in another the same summons produces silence and a shared doom (18:52 — *“And ˹beware of˺ the Day He will say, “Call upon those you claimed were My associate-gods.””*). A third passage records the moment when the partners are asked where they are, and the worshippers themselves deny the association they had maintained (41:47–48 — *“And ˹consider˺ the Day He will call to them, “Where are My ˹so-called˺ associate-gods?””*), while the gods they invoked turn on them and call them liars (16:86 — *“These are our associate-gods that we used to invoke besides You.””*).

The witness the Book recommends instead is named in a short exchange recorded elsewhere: asked who is the best witness, the Prophet ﷺ is instructed to answer that God is. To state that He is a witness between him and the audience, and that the revelation came to warn them and whoever it reaches (6:19 — *“Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Who is the best witness?””*). The verse is precise about where valid testimony is kept. A community that spent its arguments assembling supporters is being shown the only testimony that will be entered in the case.

The Book reports that argument in the words of its users: told to follow what God revealed, they answered that they would follow what their forefathers practised, and the reply asks whether they would do so even if their forefathers had no understanding or guidance (2:170 — *“˹Would they still do so,˺ even if their forefathers had ˹absolutely˺ no understanding or guidance”*).

A similar exchange is reported of the elites of earlier societies, who said that they had found their ancestors on a way and were walking in their footsteps (43:22–23 — *“In fact, they say, “We found our forefathers following a ˹particular˺ way, and we are following in their footsteps.””*), and another verse records the community's claim that what their forefathers practised was good enough for them (5:104 — *“When it is said to them, “Come to Allah’s revelations and to the Messenger,” they reply, “What we found our forefathers practicing is good enough for us.””*).
verses.42:
> ˹Beware of˺ the Day the Shin ˹of Allah˺ will be bared, and the wicked will be asked to prostrate, but they will not be able to do so

**The Idiom of the Bared Shin**

The phrase translated *the Shin will be bared* is an Arabic expression for a matter of extreme seriousness, and the commentators explain its origin in the clothing of the desert. A man wearing a long garment who sets out on strenuous work, or who finds himself in battle, gathers the cloth up so that his lower leg is exposed, and the phrase describing a crisis — that the war broke out upon the shank — comes from that picture. The verse therefore announces the arrival of a moment which no one can meet casually, and it announces it in the phrase of the audience's own daily life rather than in the abstract language of theology.

The word has a concrete counterpart elsewhere in the Book. When the queen of Sheba is brought into Solomon's palace and mistakes the crystal floor for water, the translation describes her as baring her legs (27:44 — *“But when she saw the hall, she thought it was a body of water, so she bared her legs.”*) — a person exposed before a prophet in a moment of complete surprise. The Qur'an uses the limb in its ordinary sense in that scene and reserves the phrase here, where what is exposed is not a body but a situation.

**The Body Used to Display a Spiritual Condition**

The Qur'an often indicates an inner state through the body's posture, and this passage is one of its clearest examples. In another sūrah the people who denied the truth are described as being dragged into Hell on their faces and as furthest from the right way (25:34 — *“Those who will be dragged into Hell on their faces will be in the worst place, and are ˹now˺ farthest from the ˹Right˺ Way”*); the physical position matches the fact that they spent their lives with no view of the road. Elsewhere the Book describes faces that are bright and laughing beside faces covered in dust and gloom (80:38–41 — *“On that Day ˹some˺ faces will be bright”*), and it separates the two groups by their expressions before it reports anything they said (3:106–107 — *“On that Day some faces will be bright while others gloomy.”*).

A person's habits in this world become his capacities in the next, and the inability to prostrate in this scene is the completion of a refusal rather than a punishment invented at the moment.

The same picture appears in another sūrah, where the humbling of the eyes and the covering of disgrace are described for those who are summoned (70:44 — *“with eyes downcast, utterly covered with disgrace. That is the Day they have ˹always˺ been warned of”*), and the Book's consistent method is to let the posture carry the verdict. Faces are bright or dust-covered, bodies are able or unable, and the physical detail is never an arbitrary addition to the sentence. It records the state of a person whose conduct has been travelling toward that condition for the whole of his life.

**Why the Scene Follows the Courtroom Questions**

That transition from debate to event is the sūrah's closing strategy. The verses that follow turn to the Prophet ﷺ with comfort and instruction, which means the sequence ends where the whole chapter has been leading: the verdict belongs to God, and the community's task is patience.
verses.43:
> with eyes downcast, totally covered with disgrace. For they were ˹always˺ called to prostrate ˹in the world˺ when they were fully capable ˹but they chose not to˺

**The Ability They Had**

The clause about capacity is the part of the verse that addresses the audience directly. It does not describe people who never heard the call or who were prevented from answering it; it describes men who had years of opportunity. The prayer of the Muslims was performed in the streets of Makkah, the recitation of the Qur'an included prostrations of its own, and the Prophet ﷺ had prostrated among his people for as long as they had known him. Nobody in that city could claim that the summons had been concealed, and the verse says so in a few words that leave no room for a defence.

The Arabic used for the covering suggests a garment or shade laid over a person, and the Book uses related imagery for both conditions in the next life. Faces that are bright are described with light, and faces that are ruined are described with dust and gloom (80:38–41 — *“On that Day ˹some˺ faces will be bright”*), while the people who are kept from the sight of their Lord are described as covered by a veil. The covering is not decoration; it is the closest the Book comes to a portrait of shame as a physical environment.

**What Worship Was Supposed to Do**

The same pairing of a call and a capacity appears in a parallel description of that day, where the humbling of the eyes is presented as the destination of people who had been warned about it all along (70:44 — *“with eyes downcast, utterly covered with disgrace. That is the Day they have ˹always˺ been warned of”*). The Book's warnings seldom introduce a new requirement; they remind a person of an instruction he already had. What is lost in the scene is not the opportunity but the ability to use it.

A sūrah that opens with the news of an overwhelming event describes the same expression: faces downcast on the day it arrives (88:1–2 — *“On that Day ˹some˺ faces will be downcast”*).
verses.44:
> So leave to Me ˹O Prophet˺ those who reject this message. We will gradually draw them to destruction in ways they cannot comprehend

**A Command to Hand the Matter Over**

The sūrah turns from the interrogation of the deniers to an instruction for the Prophet ﷺ. The command is to leave those who reject the reminder to God, which means ending the effort to force a verdict out of them rather than abandoning the work of warning. The Book issues the same instruction at other points in the Makkan revelation, and its purpose in each case is to relieve the messenger of a responsibility that was never his. The argument had been made; the outcome belongs to the one who will raise the question again on a day the audience does not control.

**Drawn On Gradually**

The phrase translated as *gradually draw them on* describes a process in which a person is moved forward step by step without noticing the movement. The source of the expression is the fisherman's or the traveller's experience of being brought along a gradient, and the Book uses it for the ease with which a person who reads prosperity as approval is allowed to continue. The idea is stated plainly in the sūrah of the Heavens: those who deny are left to be drawn on gradually from a direction they do not know (7:182–183 — *“As for those who deny Our signs, We will gradually draw them to destruction in ways they cannot comprehend”*).

The Book explains why the arrangement works: *“Do they think, since We provide them with wealth and children, that We hasten to ˹honour˺ them ˹with˺ all kinds of good? No! They are not aware.”* (23:55–56). The gifts themselves become the instrument of the process, because the recipient reads them as evidence about his standing.

The same sentence recurs in the Heights, where the drawing on of the deniers is followed by a statement about the delayed end and the flawless planning (7:183 — *“I ˹only˺ delay their end for a while, but My planning is flawless”*). The two verses form a pair there, and the sūrah under discussion repeats them as a pair as well. Such repetition suggests that the temptation being addressed is constant rather than occasional: comfort, success, and years of unbroken routine make a delay look like a verdict.

**The Report About Respite**

The interpretive tradition connects this verse with a report in which the Prophet ﷺ said that God grants the wrongdoer respite. That when He seizes him there is no escape, after which he recited the verse about the seizing of towns while they were doing wrong and described that seizing as painful and severe (11:102 — *“Such is the ˹crushing˺ grip of your Lord when He seizes the societies entrenched in wrongdoing. Indeed, His grip is ˹terribly˺ painful and severe”*). The report belongs to the same idea as the verse under discussion. The delay is not a gap in the divine administration of affairs; it is part of the method, and its purpose is not acquittal.

**Why Gradual Ruin Is Harder Than Sudden Ruin**

There is a reason the Book describes this process as worse than a sudden judgement arriving on time. A punishment that arrives immediately leaves the offender in the middle of his career with a clear knowledge of what has happened. A man allowed to continue has the opportunity to add to what he will be asked about, and every month of continuation confirms him in the belief that nothing is being recorded. The Book states the underlying arithmetic elsewhere, warning the deniers not to imagine that the respite granted to them is good for them: they are granted time only to increase in sin, and their punishment will be humiliating (3:178 — *“Those who disbelieve should not think that living longer is good for them. They are only given more time to increase in sin, and they will suffer a humiliating punishment”*).
verses.45:
> I ˹only˺ delay their end for a while, but My planning is flawless

**The Delay Named in the First Person**

The verse continues the previous sentence and speaks in God's own voice. The interval that the deniers experienced as security is described here as a delay granted by the one who is deciding the matter, and the second clause explains what is being done during it. The audience in Makkah had watched years pass without the punishment they mocked, and the verse names the arrangement directly rather than leaving the silence unexplained.

The word rendered *delay* covers more than time passing. It describes an extension granted to a debtor, and the commercial flavour of the term suits a sūrah addressed to traders who understood exactly what an extension meant.

**The Same Sentence in the Heights**

The Book states almost this same sentence in the sūrah of the Heights, immediately after the statement that those who deny the signs will be drawn on gradually without understanding: *“As for those who deny Our signs, We will gradually draw them to destruction in ways they cannot understand. I ˹only˺ delay their end for a while, but My planning is flawless.”* (7:182–183). The repetition of the wording is a signal. When the Qur'an uses an identical sentence in two places, the second occurrence gives the reader a way to recognise the pattern in the first, and here the repetition establishes the delay as a standing feature of how the Book describes the treatment of denial.

**Mistaking Delay for Acquittal**

The Book addresses the mistake directly and in advance: *“Those who disbelieve should not think that living longer is good for them. They are only given more time to increase in sin, and they will suffer a humiliating punishment.”* (3:178). The arrangement described there is the one in this passage. The added time is not neutral; it is time in which a record continues to be written, and the person receiving it is the author of what is being added.

**"My Planning Is Flawless"**

The term rendered *planning* is the Arabic *kayd*, a word the Book also uses for the stratagems that human beings devised against the messengers. Its use here is carefully placed. The men who were organising opposition to the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah were matching themselves against a plan made by the one who arranges every cause in the world. The Book records the same contrast at the moment of the migration: they planned, and God also planned, and God is the best of planners (8:30 — *“And ˹remember, O Prophet,˺ when the disbelievers conspired to capture, kill, or exile you. They planned, but Allah also planned. And Allah is the best of planners”*).

Elsewhere the Book applies the same vocabulary to the plotters of every generation, noting that they made a plan while a plan was being made for them without their knowledge (27:50 — *“And ˹so˺ they made a plan, but We too made a plan, while they were unaware”*). Asking the question that closes the subject: could anyone have felt secure against God's planning, when none feels secure except those who are lost (7:99 — *“Did they feel secure against Allah’s planning? None would feel secure from Allah’s planning except the losers”*)? The clause about the plan being flawless adds that nothing in it can be blocked, hurried, or redirected by the people it is directed at.
verses.46:
> Or are you asking them for a reward ˹for the message˺ so that they are overburdened by debt

**The Question Turned Back on the Messenger**

Having examined the claims of the audience, the sūrah asks about the messenger's own position. The question is whether he is charging them for the message, in a way that would burden them with an obligation and explain their refusal to accept it. The form is deliberately public. Nobody in Makkah could name a price they had been asked to pay, and the answer to the question was already known in every household that had heard him recite.

**The Book's Repeated Statements of the Same Point**

The Qur'an clears its messenger of any charge in several sūrahs, which suggests how persistent the accusation was. One passage asks the same question in a different form: *“Or ˹is it because˺ you ˹O Prophet˺ are asking them for tribute? But the reward of your Lord is best, for He is the Best Provider.”* (23:72). Another joins the absence of a charge to the purpose of the revelation: *“even though you are not asking them for a reward for this ˹Quran˺. It is only a reminder to the whole world.”* (12:104).

The identical question appears word for word in another sūrah (52:40 — *“Or are you ˹O Prophet˺ asking them for a reward ˹for the message˺ so that they are overburdened by debt”*), and the Book elsewhere invites its audience to keep whatever reward they imagine was asked of them, since the messenger's reward comes from God alone and He is a witness over everything (34:47 — *“Say, “If I had ever asked you for a reward, you could keep it. My reward is only from Allah. And He is a Witness over all things.””*). In one passage the Prophet ﷺ is told to state the alternative arrangement plainly: he asks for no reward, and whoever wishes may take a path to his Lord (25:57 — *“Say, “I do not ask you for any reward for this ˹message˺, but whoever wishes, let them pursue the Way to their Lord.””*).

**Why the Answer Matters for the Message**

A teacher paid by his students is accountable to them, and the Book's insistence that its messenger took nothing protects the content of what he delivered. Had he been paid, the message would have been open to the suspicion of tailoring, and his audience would have had a reason to examine which parts of it were designed to please the customers. The reminder arrived unattached to any human interest, and the Book treats that quality as part of its authority.

The one request the Qur'an does attach to the message is not a payment. In one verse the Prophet ﷺ is told to ask for no reward except affection among kin (42:23 — *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “I do not ask you for a reward for this ˹message˺—only honour for ˹our˺ kinship.””*), and in another the reward he mentions is offered back to the people themselves. The relationship being proposed was never a transaction, and the verse under discussion removes the last suggestion that it was.

The final verse of the sūrah describes the revelation as a reminder for all the worlds, and this verse prepares that description by taking away every trace of a price. A reminder is given freely. A person who is being reminded of something important may resent the reminder, but he cannot claim that the one reminding him is collecting a fee, and the Book keeps its own account of the matter clear in passage after passage. The trading community of the city understood commission, credit, and the difference between a gift and a contract, and its members had dealings with soothsayers, clients, and allies that ran on reciprocity.
verses.47:
> Or do they have access to ˹the Record in˺ the unseen, so they copy it ˹for all to see˺

**The Claim to Have Read the Unseen**

The interrogation reaches its highest point. The verse asks whether the audience has access to the hidden record and transcribes from it, which is a claim far beyond anything a reader might have imagined. The commentators explain the question as a challenge to the idea that the deniers' statements about the next world were as good as revelation, since a person who copies from the record in the unseen would have exactly the standing they claimed. The Book describes that record in another sūrah as being preserved in a tablet (85:22 — *“˹recorded˺ in a Preserved Tablet”*).

**The Ladder the Book Refuses Them**

The image of access to the unseen is developed elsewhere with the same bluntness. One passage asks whether the audience owns the treasuries of God or controls anything, and then supplies the only method by which the knowledge they claimed could be obtained: *“Or do they have a stairway, by which they eavesdrop ˹on the heavens˺? Then let those who do so bring a compelling proof.”* (52:38). A listener who wanted information from the sky needed a ladder and a hearing that passed the guards, and the verse invites the claimants to produce their evidence.

The Book repeatedly describes the heavens as guarded against tries of that kind, and the sūrah of the Pen's own earlier verses belong to the same picture.

**The Unseen Is Not Distributed**

The revelation is consistent about where knowledge of the hidden is kept. God alone has the keys of the unseen; the Book assigns to Him the knowledge of the Hour, the rain, the womb, and what a person will earn tomorrow (31:34 — *“Indeed, Allah ˹alone˺ has the knowledge of the Hour.”*). Even the messengers receive only what they are given, and the Qur'an's own reports of the next world are announcements made by the one who knows rather than discoveries made by anyone who looked.

**The Illusion of Self-Sufficiency**

The source of that confidence is named by the Book in a very short passage: *“Most certainly, one exceeds all bounds once they think they are selfsufficient.”* (96:6–7). The sentence describes the psychological mechanism behind every claim of the kind being examined here. A person who believes he needs nothing from anyone else will not accept that a category of knowledge exists which he cannot reach, and he will fill the gap with the conclusions that suit him.
verses.48:
> So be patient with your Lord’s decree, and do not be like ˹Jonah,˺ the Man of the Whale, who cried out ˹to Allah˺, in total distress

**The Man of the Whale**

The prophet being cited is Jonah, and the Book devotes a passage to his story in the sūrah of those ranged in ranks. He was one of the messengers (37:139 — *“And Jonah was indeed one of the messengers”*), he fled to a loaded ship (37:140 — *“˹Remember˺ when he fled to the overloaded ship”*), the lot was drawn and he was thrown overboard (37:141 — *“Then ˹to save it from sinking,˺ he drew straws ˹with other passengers˺. He lost ˹and was thrown overboard˺”*), and the whale swallowed him while he was blameworthy (37:142 — *“Then the whale engulfed him while he was blameworthy”*). His survival is attributed to a habit he had maintained: *“Had he not ˹constantly˺ glorified ˹Allah˺, he would have certainly remained in its belly until the Day of Resurrection.”* (37:143–144). He was then cast onto an open shore, worn out, and a plant was made to grow over him (37:145–146 — *“But We cast him onto the open ˹shore˺, ˹totally˺ worn out”*).

The comparison is not an accusation. The Book places the example of a prophet directly beside the instruction given to the Prophet ﷺ, and the effect is to normalise the strain he was under while ruling out the response it was producing. A man being told not to behave like Jonah has been told that his situation resembles Jonah's, and the resemblance is a kind of company.

The story also illustrates how much of a messenger's work is waiting. Jonah is described in the Book as one of the messengers (37:139 — *“And Jonah was indeed one of the messengers”*), and the account of his mission consists almost completely of his departure and his recovery, with the response of his city mentioned in a single verse from another sūrah (10:98 — *“If only there had been a society which believed ˹before seeing the torment˺ and, therefore, benefited from its belief, like the people of Jonah. When they believed, We lifted from them the torment of disgrace in this world and allowed them enjoyment for a while”*). The work between the call and the response takes up no narrative at all, which is exactly the part of the assignment that this verse is addressing.

**The Cry in Total Distress**

The adjective describing Jonah's call describes a man in the grip of grief, and the Book records what he said: *“And ˹remember˺ when the Man of the Whale stormed off ˹from his city˺ in a rage, thinking We would not restrain him. Then in the ˹veils of˺ darkness he cried out, “There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except You. Glory be to You! I have certainly done wrong.””* (21:87). The prayer combines the confession of God's uniqueness with an admission of his own fault, and the next verse reports the answer: *“So We answered his prayer and rescued him from anguish. And so do We save the ˹true˺ believers.”* (21:88).

The Prophet ﷺ is being shown a messenger who had to be rescued, and the sūrah's prohibition is a warning against putting himself in the position of needing such a rescue.

One verse tells him that his patience is only possible with God's help and that he should not grieve over the disbelievers or be distressed by their schemes (16:127 — *“Be patient ˹O Prophet˺, for your patience is only with Allah’s help. Do not grieve over those ˹who disbelieve˺, nor be distressed by their schemes”*).

Another reminds him of the pattern of earlier messengers, who were rejected and persecuted and endured until help arrived, with the assurance that God's promise is never broken (6:34 — *“And Allah’s promise ˹to help˺ is never broken.”*).
verses.49:
> Had he not been shown grace by his Lord, he would have certainly been cast onto the open ˹shore˺, still blameworthy

**The Shore and the Plant**

What actually happened to him is described with attention to his condition after the rescue. He was cast onto an open shore, worn out, and then a plant was made to grow over him (37:145–146 — *“But We cast him onto the open ˹shore˺, ˹totally˺ worn out”*). The Book's care for the mechanism of recovery is characteristic.

The sūrah of the Prophets reports the response to his prayer in the same spirit: his call was answered, he was rescued from anguish, and the Book adds that this is how the believers are saved (21:88 — *“So We answered his prayer and rescued him from anguish. And so do We save the ˹true˺ believers”*).

The passage shows a pattern that appears throughout the Book. Rescue is the first stage, and rehabilitation is the second. A person is brought out of the consequence of his conduct, and then work is done on him so that he is fit for what comes next. Joseph was brought out of the well and the prison before he was given authority; Moses was brought out of the river before he was given the mission; Jonah was brought out of the whale and then shaded and fed.

The verse's counterfactual marks the difference between the two stages.

It also fixes the limit of what a rescue can accomplish by itself. A person may be brought out of a bad situation and remain in the condition that produced it, and the sentence says exactly that about a prophet: without the favour of his Lord, the man on the shore would have been the same man who went over the side.

The verses about Jonah move from the admission of wrongdoing in the darkness (21:87 — *“And ˹remember˺ when the Man of the Whale stormed off ˹from his city˺ in a rage, thinking We would not restrain him. Then in the ˹veils of˺ darkness he cried out, “There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except You. Glory be to You! I have certainly done wrong.””*) through rescue to a fresh commission.
verses.50:
> Then his Lord chose him, making him one of the righteous

**Election After Failure**

The verse completes the story with an act of selection. The man who had fled, been swallowed, and been rescued was then chosen by his Lord and placed among the righteous, and the sūrah's order is deliberate. Election comes after the episode, not before it, and the sequence is what the Book presents to a messenger under pressure in Makkah. A fault that has been dealt with does not close a man's file. It becomes the setting of the next appointment.

The Arabic verb rendered *chose him* is the one the Book uses for God's selection of individuals for a task, and it appears in connection with a small number of prophets. Being chosen in this vocabulary is not a reward for merit already showed; it is an assignment granted by the one entitled to grant it. The same word stands behind the selection of the prophets generally, and its use here in the aftermath of Jonah's mistake is the point of the verse.

The mercy that balances the warnings is also the reason the verse can end the story where it does. A revelation that threatened without offering rescue would misrepresent the One who sent it, and the sūrah's final pages are carefully arranged so that the listener hears the warning and the way out in the same sitting.
verses.51:
> The disbelievers would almost cut you down with their eyes when they hear ˹you recite˺ the Reminder, and say, “He is certainly a madman.”

**The Gaze That Almost Strikes**

The verse describes hostility that has become physical without becoming violent. The eyes of the disbelievers, fixed on the Prophet ﷺ as he recites, are said to come close to cutting him down, and the image treats a look as an instrument capable of damage. The context is a public recitation: the message being recited is the reminder, and the men listening are not indifferent to it. Their reaction is intense enough that the Book describes it in the language of an attack.

The Book treats looking as an act with moral weight of its own. Believers are commanded to *“lower their gaze and guard their chastity”* (24:30), an instruction that assumes a person answers for what he fixes his eyes on. When the same Book describes the mockers' eyes almost cutting the reciter down, it is reporting a hostility that has already begun in the will and is only waiting for the power to complete itself.

**The Charge of Madness Returns**

The verse reports the accusation that had been made against the Prophet ﷺ from the earliest days in Makkah. The sūrah's opening had already answered it: the Prophet ﷺ is addressed at the start of this chapter as not being, by the grace of his Lord, a madman, and is described as having an outstanding character. The charge appears at the beginning and at the end of the sūrah, which is how the Book frames a smear it intends to leave dismantled.
verses.52:
> But it is simply a reminder to the whole world

**For the Whole World**

The reminder is not addressed to one clan or one language, and the Book states the universality of the mission in several places. The Prophet ﷺ is described as having been sent as a mercy for the whole world (21:107 — *“We have sent you ˹O Prophet˺ only as a mercy for the whole world”*), and the same expression used here appears in the sūrah of Joseph, where the message is described as a reminder to the whole world in the middle of an argument about its messenger's honesty (12:104 — *“even though you are not asking them for a reward for this ˹Quran˺. It is only a reminder to the whole world”*). The Book's own account of its audience has never been tribal, even when its first hearers were members of a tribe.

The universality claimed here is not a general statement about the worth of human beings; it is a statement about the scope of the warning. Every community that receives the message is being told what it needs to know about its own condition, and the sūrah has addressed its audience on that basis throughout, moving from the Makkans' own admissions about creation to arguments they could follow about their own trade. The reminder operates in the language and reasoning of the people it reaches, which is why the Book describes its messengers as speaking to their peoples in their own terms.

A second reading of the verse, reported by the commentators, takes the reminder to be the person of the Prophet ﷺ himself rather than the text he recites. The two readings agree on the substance: either the recitation is a warning offered to all peoples, or the man delivering it is, and the audience's mockery is directed at a benefit intended for them.

The chapter's contents make the closing description of the message precise. It has reminded its hearers that a record is being written and that a day of reckoning is coming. That the man delivering the message is of outstanding character. That a garden's owners lost everything by shutting the poor out; that a series of claims about the Hereafter had no document behind them; that the wicked will be unable to prostrate; and that a prophet who ran away was rescued and restored. Each of those is a reminder in the strict sense of the word: something known, neglected, and brought back into view.

The commentators note a second possible reading of the verse, according to which the reminder being described is not the message but the man who delivers it, since the Prophet ﷺ is himself called a reminder in other passages. Both readings agree on the substance. Either the recitation is a reminder for all the worlds, or the messenger is one, and the sūrah's audience is left with the same fact: what they were mocking was a benefit offered to them and to everyone else.

**Why the Chapter Ends Here**

The sentence is not confined to this closing position. It stands in Sūrah Ṣād as the answer to the arguments about the messenger (38:87 — *“It is only a reminder to the whole world”*), and it appears in al-Takwīr alongside the description of the revelation's delivery (81:27 — *“Surely this ˹Quran˺ is only a reminder to the whole world”*). In each placement the same words settle the same suspicion about who the Qurʾān is for, and here they are the last thing the mockers hear before the sūrah ends.
